A key factor contributing to the diversity in sizes and compositions of terrestrial exoplanets is thought to be the core composition of protoplanetary cores during accretion. This study aims to explore core structures in models of star-planet systems by leveraging high-resolution spectra to determine elemental abundances in stars hosting terrestrial planets. By incorporating these abundances into theoretical models of protoplanetary cores, we gain insight into the core's development and its potential influence on planetary formation. Our analysis of 15 stars featuring terrestrial exoplanets yielded 11 new core metallicity estimates, 7 of which fell within the range considered typical for chondritic objects, while the remaining 4 had significantly higher core metallicity. This led us to identify two subgroups of stars with terrestrial planets: typical-chondritic core metallicity is a characteristic shared by stars hosting small terrestrial planets, whereas stars hosting larger planets tend to have more metal-rich cores. One possible connection is that larger planets may have been formed through processes requiring core heat to drive differentiation and melt rock, or through the capture of metal-rich planetary building blocks. However, more in-depth investigations into various planetary formation mechanisms are required to link core metallicity to the characteristics of planets discovered thus far.

Deep learning-based wireless positioning technology utilizes CSI data to determine user location in an indoor environment. However, CSI is a noisy and unstable measurement which complicates the training of deep learning models and leads to reduced accuracy. Focusing on the inherent spatial characteristics within CSI data rather than raw CSI itself has yielded improved results. Nevertheless, current methods overlook the varying propagation channels between individual CSI values, thereby discarding potentially useful information. This can lead to increased noise during positioning, lowering the overall accuracy. To resolve this, we introduce a novel AE_CSI method that leverages attention-enhanced CSI data for higher accuracy in location determination. Our proposed approach first separates the CSI data into individual subpackets, evaluates the propagation channel between each subpacket, and selects the optimal subpacket CSI values that maximize signal strength. These selected values are then averaged to produce a stable CSI signal. To extract spatial characteristics, we employ an attention mechanism that matches subpacket CSI values with spatial bases, resulting in enhanced spatial information. Experimental results show that our AE_CSI method achieves improved accuracy in location determination, outperforming existing methods.

Building on a previous approach that expanded modal logic to integrated systems with multiple operators, this paper expands on that method to cover a diverse set of modal logics within pretopological spaces, providing a unified framework that encompasses a wide range of known categories. By categorifying the semantics of these logics, the paper establishes theorems and proofs analogous to those found in the axiomatic method. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the duality between algebra and geometry inherent in the pretopological framework, revealing relationships between topological properties and logical principles.

In 2007, Harrow and Strader introduced the concept of edge-tinted paths in bipartite graphs, where each edge is given a distinct color. Their result implied that a certain linear equation system had solutions. Later, researchers generalized this finding to cubic bipartite graphs, establishing stronger conclusions about the same equation system. However, despite these advancements, the original question of whether the equation system has solutions for planar bipartite graphs remained unsolved. Our study presents a counterexample - an edge-tinted cubic bipartite graph that does not yield a solution for the given equation system. This counterexample also reveals the validity of a particular conjecture involving the connected sum operation.

We examine functions of odd permutation symmetry defined on the Hamming graphs of dimension $n$. These functions have their values determined by the eigenvalues of specific matrices resulting from the adjacency graph. We investigate under which conditions such functions can be expressed as sums of products of eigenvalues and permutation symbols, given the restriction that certain spectral parameters are utilized. Our research enables the quantification of a particular type of function support, ultimately leading to the development of an algorithm for identifying the minimum support size among all functions meeting the specified spectral criteria.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To overcome compatibility and update issues, a decision was made to create a browser-based version. The ShinyCOPASI project involved rewriting COPASI using R and Shiny, making it accessible via a web interface. This new version enables users to explore and interact with models in the browser, without needing to install anything. Users can access important COPASI features through tabs, including model editing, simulation settings, and analytical results. The successful implementation of ShinyCOPASI not only addresses usability concerns but also opens up opportunities for integrating the model viewer with other bioinformatics tools.

Measuring ambiguity in human intelligence is relatively straightforward, with clear, well-established metrics that reflect performance in relevant situations. In contrast, evaluating ambiguity in machine learning is more complex, with various definitions and metrics lacking a standardized consensus. This study provides a comprehensive overview of current research regarding the measurement of ambiguity in machine learning, particularly focusing on classification and self-supervised models. It examines different approaches to ambiguity representation, categorizes existing metrics based on widely held assumptions about machine learning, and assesses the effectiveness of widely used metrics in relevant applications, including model interpretability and robustness. The analysis offers perspectives on how to address the lack of a unified ambiguity metric and suggests potential future research directions.

We compute the closed subalgebras, denoted as ${\mathcal C}_n$, of central elements within the tensor C*-algebra ${\mathcal O}_n$, associated with finite compact quantum groups ${\mathbb G}_n$. It is observed that these subalgebras constitute non-degenerate, invariant subalgebras under the comultiplication $\Delta$ of ${\mathcal O}_n$. Furthermore, we establish that the subalgebra ${\mathfrak C}(\Delta)$, consisting of central elements in $\bigoplus_{n}\mathcal C_n$, is dense in the von Neumann algebra $\Gamma({\mathbb G})''$ and that it is a *-subalgebra of $\Gamma({\mathbb G})''$. We also show that the subalgebra ${\mathfrak C}(\Delta)$ is neither a commutative subalgebra nor a Hopf *-algebra in general, but it does contain the commutative subalgebra ${\mathfrak C}(\epsilon)$.

In solving large-scale extensive Markov decision processes, the computational burden can be overwhelming due to the size of the reward matrix, but using these problems as linear complementarity problems allows for efficient solutions through the GMRES method, especially when coupled with strategy iteration for optimal solutions. However, the economic cost of generating and storing residual information for each iteration becomes prohibitively expensive for very large problems. This research proposes modifying GMRES with an imprecision limit on error tolerance, effectively reducing memory and computational demands without significantly affecting solution quality. The new approach is compared to traditional GMRES and strategy iteration methods, demonstrating superior performance in handling extensive Markov decision processes.

Consider a weighted directed graph $(\V, \E)$ where each edge is assigned a positive integer weight. Let's define an ideal $\I$ generated by the edges in a linearly independent subset of the graph's vertices. In this study, we're interested in symbolic and common Hauptideals of this ideal, especially its weighted version. These ideals have significant mathematical implications, particularly in the fields of algebra, topology, and chemistry, making their study vital. Our research explores the nature of these ideals, particularly in edge configurations that are either generic (generic configurations) or specific to homomorphic images of the given graph. For generic configurations, we establish both positive and limiting results regarding the cardinality of the defining Stanley-Reisner ideal, while for non-generic configurations, we focus on the ideal's prime divisors and the number of prime factors. Our investigation also examines the feasibility of prime divisors having specific powers and whether they form a minimal generating set. Additionally, we delve into the common Hauptideal's height and the symbolic Hauptideal's degree.

When computer simulations yield time series outcomes, researchers face the challenge of identifying the underlying model parameters that produce these results, a reverse problem with limited analytical solutions. We have developed a novel approach to address this issue using multiple contour assessment. By applying this method to a simulation involving a neurodegenerative disease model, we were able to demonstrate its efficacy and calculate distribution estimates for the model parameters. The multiple contour assessment method combines simulated annealing and multiple imputation to generate a large number of parameter estimates, which are then grouped into contours based on their similarity. We have shown that the variability within these contours is negligible, thereby eliminating the need for variance estimation. The contour approach also facilitates the identification of problematic simulations by flagging areas with high variability. We have observed that the variability within the contours is heavily influenced by the diagnostic metric used, prompting further investigation of this relationship.

To achieve reliable machine learning in the face of unforeseen challenges, also known as out-of-distribution (OOD) challenges, we must incorporate robust training methods. By incorporating data from multiple geographic and demographic regions during training, models can gain resistance to local biases and enhance their generalizability. However, the impact of regional diversity on the development of resilient models remains unclear, as prior research often trains and tests models within the same regional context.

In our research, we examine how training with data from one region (source domain) and testing with data from another region (target domain) affects a model's performance. By leveraging synthetic data generated with Normalized Adversarial Examples, we simulate target domain data without requiring actual labels, thus expanding the scope of research into cross-regional robustness. Through our analysis, we discover that regional diversity benefits certain models, but can harm others by exacerbating their existing weaknesses. As a result, we propose the use of cross-region evaluation as a crucial evaluation metric for assessing the efficacy of robust training methods.

Ultimately, we find that principled and targeted data augmentation strategies remain the most reliable method for enhancing a model's resistance to OOD challenges, but also highlight the value of cross-region evaluation as a supplementary metric for evaluating the robustness of machine learning models.

High-energy particles known as jets produced in collisions between lead ions at the LHC have been studied to gain insights into how these interactions affect the formation of jets in dense environments. In simulations, it's shown that alterations in the direction of a jet and changes in the particles that make up the jet can both contribute to alterations in its structure. This research uses data from the CMS experiment and places these findings into context by comparing them to simulations of normal collisions, while also accounting for alterations in the particles that form the jet. The study finds that alterations in this context are linked to alterations in the direction of a jet, but does not see the expected level of alterations in the particles that form the jet within a specified range of modifications in the direction of a jet. The study also finds that alterations in this context are linked to alterations in the direction of a jet, but does not see the expected level of alterations in the particles that form the jet outside of this range of modifications in the direction of a jet. The study places these findings into context by comparing them to simulations of normal collisions.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted an intriguing link between Apéry-type inverse binomial series and colored multiple zeta values. Building upon previous findings that established this connection for specific types of series, this study expands on this relationship by exploring more general cases, specifically: (1) a broader class of inverse binomial series based on the fundamental idea of Henle and Tschirner and (2) a particular series related to the fundamental idea of Guo, Zhang, and the second author. The results shown here not only predict but also explain the rationality of the coefficients in these series, thereby providing a theoretical justification for the observed patterns. Moreover, this study delves deeper into the underlying mechanisms by clarifying and extending previous conjectures regarding the Apéry-type inverse binomial series.

Initial reports suggested that WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, a previously known brown dwarf, exhibited mysterious variability, with some speculating it might be an ejected or young T Tauri star. We investigated this claim by collecting near-infrared photometry data from the past four years as part of the NEOWISE-RR survey. Contrary to expectations, the brown dwarf's behavior matched predictions for an ordinary quiescent brown dwarf, with seasonal fluctuations seen in 2 micrometer observations. It's worth noting that initial inaccuracies in WISEA J153429.75-104303.3's data likely stemmed from a nearby star's influence on 3 micrometer WISE images, causing what appeared to be variability.

The relativistic heavy-ion collisions research has generated a substantial amount of data for hadron production in collisions involving large nuclei, but a comprehensive and precise theoretical model for hadron production is yet to be established. In this study, a Strangeness Equilibrium Model and a state-of-the-art relativistic transport simulation, called PHENOMENISM, are combined to predict hadron production in Xe-Xe collisions at distinct center-of-mass energies. By effectively accounting for nucleon-nucleon interactions and transverse momentum distributions, this theoretical framework yields precise predictions for mass yields, mean transverse momentum, and rapidity distributions. Furthermore, this model is utilized to investigate mass production yields in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV, 29.3 TeV, and 54.4 TeV, as well as 200 GeV in Au-Au collisions, providing a benchmark for comparison with future experimental results.

The evolution of parton distribution functions at various scales is governed by renormalization group equations, with solutions that depend on past history. In many cases, explicit solutions are not available, making it necessary to use approximation theorems. The concept of effective renormalization, established in a previous study, will be extended to the PDF evolution equations, incorporating concepts from functional renormalization. The goal is to create a theoretical framework that allows for the progression of PDF from a knowledge of lower-scale distributions to higher-scale distributions, with potential applications in quantifying PDF uncertainties. A case study will be conducted using the PDF from a lattice QCD calculation at a low scale and tracking its progression to a higher scale.

Specimens made from simulated Martian and Lunar soil mixes were pressed and fired at various temperatures, ranging between 600$\circ$F to 1200$\circ$F (approximately 320 to 660$\circ$C) to study their structure and strength. X-ray computed tomography was used to analyze the internal structure of the specimens, and compressive strength was the property that was evaluated. The results showed a notable improvement in the strength of the specimens fired between 600$\circ$F and 900$\circ$F (approximately 320 to 480$\circ$C), which is the range suitable for 3D printing, indicating a promising future for in-situ and additive manufacturing techniques on the Moon and Mars.

When a liquid layer is formed on a fiber and subjected to an axial disturbance, it experiences instability under specific conditions determined by the static liquid profile and surface tension. This study investigates how surface tension is affected when one of the liquid-solid interfaces is subjected to a low-friction coating, resulting in reduced capillary forces. A theoretical model has been developed to analyze the instability in the absence of surface tension. Numerical simulations revealed that a low-friction interface can cause the liquid profile to deviate significantly even at very weak surface tension levels. Consequently, this surface tension can still play a crucial role in determining the critical wave number for instability, whereas the resulting liquid droplets can differ significantly from the traditional Rayleigh-Plateau scenario.

We suggest revisiting the standard method of estimating star formation rates by using specific recombination lines and strong dust features in galaxies. This is done by comparing observed data with models that include both star formation and dust extinction processes. Our argument centers on the reliability of a particular line, Brackett-$\gamma$, as an SFR indicator. By referencing previous studies, we show that this line is just as reliable as other lines, such as H$_2$. Like other lines, it serves as a direct physical connection between star formation rates and observed emission and can be compared across different environments. Our conclusion is that using star formation rates based on line diagnostics is more accurate than those derived from SED fittings, especially in environments that are not perfectly ordered.

In the realm of $\mathcal{O}^{s\l}\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{gl}_N)$, a domain within the type $I^*$ sector of the Ginzburg algebra, we identify a subalgebra consisting of elements that commute with the Fock-Chevalley $E_{11}$ generator, denoted as $\mathfrak{sl}_{II}^+$. This subalgebra is found to possess a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$-graded structure, with its two components serving as quantum com-algebras, specifically isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}_{N/2}(\mathbb{C})$ and $\mathfrak{sl}_N(\mathbb{C})$. Furthermore, we establish connections between the $\mathfrak{sl}_{II}^{+}$ algebra and regional $\mathfrak{gl}_{N+1}$ module symmetries. These relationships enable us to define a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$-graded tensor product * of the type $I^*$ sector's Fock-Chevalley algebra, as well as its linear dual. This construction allows us to define a homomorphism $\Phi$ from the ungraded tensor product $\mathfrak{gl}_{I^*}^{+}\otimes\mathfrak{gl}_{\bar{I}^*}^{+}$ to the * algebra

Our approach to diffusion provides a comprehensive framework for modeling complex phenomena governed by Fourier's law. We establish a one-parameter group of linear transformations, $\{S_t\}_{t\geq0}$, where each evolution $S_t$ preserves the convex nature of the diffusion equation. Consequently, its natural boundary conditions are preserved as well. We utilize this transformation to develop solutions for the Dirichlet problem under specified conditions, especially when the data satisfies a uniform Sobolev regularity. Notably, our method enables the construction of a universal solution for the Dirichlet problem with data in $C(\bar{\Omega})$, where $\Omega$ is a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\geq1$.

This work addresses the UEC 2021 Mathematical Handwriting Recognition Challenge by focusing on key aspects of mathematical expression recognition. Our approach differs from conventional methods by utilizing token-level features instead of the traditional symbol-level focus. This shift allows for the incorporation of more sophisticated feature engineering methods, enabling better performance. Specifically, we've developed three unique feature sets, including those based on the sensitivity of handwriting devices, spatial relationships between characters, and character connectivity, which are all leveraged to achieve exceptional results. During the challenge evaluation, our proposed features demonstrated outstanding accuracy, earning top honors in the test set with a score of 81.29%, ultimately securing 3rd place overall.

This study presents an innovative approach to synthetic speech length manipulation, allowing for the production of extended or shortened speech lengths using a non-statistical method solely based on median values. A two-stage median calculation process is employed, starting with the estimation of unseen lengths from existing training data, followed by the generation of novel speech lengths using this estimate as a reference. Building upon the success of the initial method, an enhanced version incorporates the use of prior linguistic knowledge to further improve outcomes. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed techniques is conducted using multiple objective metrics, including statistical and non-statistical measures, in relation to the length of target canonical templates.

spHabitat is a comprehensive R tool for building single-species, multi-species, and integrated presence models that incorporate various habitat models. This package offers user-friendly functions to define study areas using polygons, calculate spatial characteristics of cells within these areas, and train models using machine learning algorithms. Users can also perform predictions and evaluations on developed models, and the package is designed to be accessible through an interactive user interface. spHabitat offers a range of features including data splitting, correlation analysis, and variable selection to facilitate easy model building and evaluation.

The Skincare initiative presents a comprehensive AI solution for diagnosing skin cancer, involving image classification, segmentation, and tumor prognosis. A dataset of 100,000 dermatological images has been assembled from the dermatologic community's expertise, allowing for the development of a sophisticated, multi-layered neural network that effectively classifies six distinct skin lesion types. Additionally, the system identifies and segments the boundaries of the lesions, providing essential context and context-free information. A modular, interactive visualization tool has been designed to facilitate communication between clinicians and the complex neural networks, while maintaining confidentiality of the assembled dataset.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from multivariate spectral data, we developed a stochastic autoencoder. By applying this model to the core of a supernova's spectrum, we can determine its intrinsic profile and then compare it to a standard reference, similar to how researchers analyze light curves. Our approach enables the quantification of individual supernovae's intrinsic variability and the derivation of a randomized standard profile for type Ia supernovae. Furthermore, this model can identify unusual supernovae and provide insights into the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae. Our findings are consistent with previous research and demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in uncovering the intrinsic patterns of type Ia supernovae from spectral data.

A massive galaxy at a distant time is seen through a gravitational lens, allowing for a clear observation of its gas release. This phenomenon provides valuable insights into the galaxy's past history and the processes within it. Data from spectrographic observations, combined with computer models, reveal two distinct regions of neutral gas emission. These regions have observed velocities of around 240 and 290 km per second, relative to the galaxy's core frame. This observation is consistent with the release of material and supports the hypothesis that the galaxy is experiencing a major star-forming event. 

Key characteristics of the observed features include narrow emissions of hydrogen and calcium, a broader hydrogen alpha line with a slower recession velocity, and a highly redshifted hydrogen beta emission. This is likely due to gas being released along our line of sight, without a corresponding shift in velocity. Both emissions exhibit similar intensities, despite being separated by a certain distance. This is consistent with the theory that the released material is in the form of gas streams. 

Data on the observed features, along with additional observations and computer models, are presented. This includes findings from ALMA, Hubble, and Spitzer telescopes, as well as a computational code developed by Krantz et al. (2022). This code uses a complex model of the galaxy's structure to simulate the observed features. 

Analysis of the observed features, along with additional observations and computer models, are presented. This includes findings from ALMA, Hubble, and Spitzer telesc

High-resolution numerical simulations of turbulent plumes that rise from a single source have been conducted to study how particles move within these plumes. The particles, represented by Lagrangian methods, have complex behaviors influenced by factors such as diffusion, buoyancy, and inertial effects. The simulations account for a wide range of particle sizes by incorporating calculations based on the Stokes number, a key parameter. The results show that smaller particles tend to follow the fluid's movement, distributing themselves throughout the plume in a smooth, symmetrical pattern. In contrast, larger particles are heavier and sink below the fluid's influence, accumulating near the base of the plume. The particles' behavior is also influenced by the presence of vortices that form at certain heights within the plume, causing particles to be swept up and depositing them in distinct rings at different altitudes. The occurrence of these particle rings can be predicted based on the particles' size and the characteristics of the vortices they become entangled in. Additionally, the simulations demonstrate that smaller particles can reach higher altitudes than larger particles, leading to distinct distributions of particles of different sizes. The occurrence of 'dust-depleted' zones at certain heights within the plume is also influenced by the particles' size, with larger particles creating these 'dust-depleted' zones at the base of the plume due to their lower mobility. The study's findings provide new insights into particle behavior and offer a classification system for predicting the particles' distribution based on

Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting a more comprehensive framework of contact patterns in terms of hypergraphs, we aim to refine our understanding of epidemic transmission. Through both theoretical and numerical analyses, we investigate how the spectral properties of the infection rate matrix relate to the degree distribution of the hypergraph. While complete graphs exhibit well-documented threshold behavior, our results for more general hypergraphs show that near-complete scenarios also display non-trivial, second-order transitions.

Recent discoveries of antiferromagnetic stability in 2D ferromagnets offer potential in producing robust and stable spin waves despite minimal magnetic loss. To explore the impact of Rashba states and chirality on the spin polarizations of electrons in such systems, we conducted an in-depth study using electron spectroscopy of a CrI$_3$ bilayer. Using time-resolved second-harmonic generation (TR-SHG) and density functional theory (DFT), we investigated the spin structure of the CrI$_3$ bilayer. Our findings reveal that Rashba-sensitive magnon excitation produces a significant anisotropy in the spin polarization of electrons. Additionally, the spin polarization pattern is significantly influenced by the magnetic configuration of the system, including spiral, circular, and helical arrangements. By adjusting the magnetic configuration, it is possible to customize the spin polarization pattern, thereby providing a means to control the spin Hall effect in 2D ferromagnetic materials at the nanoscale.

Recent discoveries of super-Jovians around low-field stars hint at possible differential rotation in these stars' interiors, and a dynamo model we've developed to study solar-type stars is being applied to hypothetical stars with anti-solar differential rotation patterns, and we've found that weakly field stars can remain weakly magnetized even in the long term, supporting the initial discovery. Additionally, our model indicates that weakly magnetized stars tend to be slowly rotating, and our results suggest that early rotational velocities of stars like K2-168b and K2-329b should be relatively high.

A significant issue in multimodal learning involves constructing a unified architecture that can process and integrate various data types while ensuring shared representations. Current designs for handling multiple data types are often limited by their ability to learn shared features, as they neglect to utilize the full potential of their respective networks. This leads to suboptimal performance when dealing with datasets of multiple modalities. To address this problem, we present the K-fan Multimodal deep learning framework, featuring a unique architecture for shared feature learning across multiple networks. By applying a kernel-based superposition model, we integrate modalities at the shared layer, leveraging the benefits of superposition to improve performance. Furthermore, we develop an unsupervised learning method for feature extraction, utilizing superposition to its fullest extent. As a result, our proposed framework demonstrates superior performance on three diverse benchmark datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in both supervised and unsupervised learning regimes.

The use of multithreaded systems is widespread in modern computing, leading to a significant need for reliable and efficient concurrency model checking tools. While advanced model checkers can handle complex programs in a short time, user-friendly and easy-to-configure tools are often necessary for educational purposes and everyday software development. Our paper introduces McMini, a state-of-the-art model verifier that employs DPOR as its underlying algorithm and offers a user-friendly interface with adjustable parameters for custom modeling and performance optimization. By refining McMini's design and operational details, we successfully applied the model checker to verify complex C programs, outperforming leading model checkers in both speed and efficiency.

The widespread circulation of false information through social media is an ongoing issue, which has been further exacerbated by private messaging services like WhatsApp. A novel approach to managing the spread of misinformation is to limit message forwarding functionality, with platforms promoting this tactic as an effective solution. In this study, we examine the potential of this policy by integrating an anti-forwarding intervention within WhatsApp, specifically in Indonesia and India during the COVID-19 vaccine and fake news crisis. Our analysis reveals that limiting message forwarding led to a significant decline in misinformation propagation, but only among users who adopted this limitation. Notably, counter-narratives aimed at correcting existing misinformation had varying levels of success, with some topics seeing little change and others exhibiting an unexpected increase in misinformation propagation. Our findings suggest that restricting message forwarding leads to an uneven distribution of misinformation propagation, where adhering users experience a substantial decrease while non-adhering users experience minimal change.

The evolution of new species or species variants typically begins with a single initial state.
A mathematical model known as general supercritical branching populations is employed to analyze the likelihood of these species becoming dominant.
The probability distribution of species' genetic diversity is examined, specifically the frequency of different genetic variants, and a statistical method is developed to estimate this distribution from population data.
The analysis considers both a continuous time model and a discrete time model with varying population size management strategies.

The use of countermeasures in speaker verification systems has become increasingly important to mitigate speaker impersonation attacks. However, the development of effective countermeasures has been hampered by the lack of accessible counterattack datasets and standardized evaluation protocols. To address this gap, we have developed a versatile countermeasure system that can operate without access to privileged information and is evaluated using the extensive Forbes dataset on speaker impersonation attacks. Our proposed system employs a deep neural network with an attentive activation mechanism that focuses on probe features unrelated to the voice, thereby significantly enhancing the system's performance. The evaluation of our system in various settings demonstrates its substantial improvement over existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of authentication accuracy and robustness.

Supergravity, combining local supersymmetry and general relativity, offers a robust framework for theoretical physics. However, supergravity models based on de Sitter space, describing cosmic scenarios like inflation, face issues with moduli incompressibility and cosmological constant problems, limiting their applicability. In contrast, effective field theories of supergravity, exempt from these issues but requiring local supersymmetry, can be utilized. This study examines locally supersymmetric effective field theories of inflation, analyzing scalar potentials and slow-roll dynamics in both canonical and canonical holomorphic forms.

Research focused on extreme astrophysical phenomena has revealed hadronic origins for gamma-ray rays with high energy in excess of millions of teraelectronvolts, stemming from particle accelerator experiments. This has led to an understanding of nature's disassociation of photon pairs, a phenomenon influenced by parameters in particle interactions, such as energy, angle, and time intervals. We investigate photon pair associations with limited time intervals and significant energy disparities, identifying asymmetry in pair distributions that correlates with energy disparities. This asymmetry, observed in Earth-based gamma-ray telescopes, could offer insight into astrophysical sources like supernovae, neutron star mergers, and cosmic accelerators.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For further development, it is crucial to gain insights into the material properties at terahertz frequencies. This can be achieved through combining near-field terahertz scanning microscopy with electrical connectivity to quantum circuit components. The study provides a detailed examination of microwave resonators made from NbAlO$_3$ and Nb, utilizing both silicon and silicon-germanium substrates. The research utilized a vector mesoanalyzer for simultaneous measurement of terahertz reflectance and microwave dissipation. The analysis offers precise identification of the material and the device boundary, as well as assessing the impact of bio-hazards and temperature variations. The research also analyzes the impact of different surface treatments on the material. The study's results contribute significantly to the characterization of superconducting quantum circuits and set a precedent for integrating advanced microscopy techniques with electrical testing of circuit components.

The question considers how the real line can be split into a set of subsets in a specific order. These subsets must adhere to specific criteria - they must all be unique, cover the entire real line, and form a sequence in a particular order. We're looking for subcollections of a specific size within this sequence, and theorems are developed to describe both the smallest and largest possible sizes for these subcollections in terms of cardinality.

This study examines the impact of introducing novel investment approaches on the performance of established strategies in financial markets. To achieve this, we utilize an agent-based model that simulates multiple groups of agents with distinct investment methods. When a new agent enters the market with an innovative strategy, we assess its effect on the existing strategies' outcomes. Our analysis indicates that the introduction of novel approaches leads to a decline in the returns of certain established strategies, while others experience enhanced performance. Interestingly, our findings also show that the response of each group to the new strategy is highly dependent on their specific characteristics. Ultimately, our research suggests that the outcome of integrating different investment methods in financial markets is complex and heavily influenced by the specifics of the market dynamics.

Recent research has shed light on the feasibility of detecting network traffic patterns using machine learning-based algorithms, specifically in identifying command-line tools employed by red teams. Our study builds upon this by targeting protocol analysis in OSINT (open-source intelligence) and examining its vulnerability to attacks. We assess the potential for malicious actors to deceive machine learning models by crafting fake tool signatures and observe that simply combining tool features can deceive certain models. Additionally, our findings indicate that leveraging low-cost, automated tools can effectively exploit weaknesses in protocol identification, where a distinct fingerprint can trick a trained model into falsely identifying a target protocol.

Electrostatic gating significantly affects the magnetic properties of two-dimensional materials, particularly through the variation of local electric fields. In this study, we examine the impact of a nearby superconductor as a gated electrode on the magnetic response in thin magnetic films. By considering high-frequency magnons, we investigate how the magnetic excitations are influenced by the variable electric field generated by the superconductor. Our analysis indicates that the magnetic modes can be efficiently modulated, resulting in notable changes to the magnetic spectrum. This research showcases the efficacy of using a superconductor as a gated electrode to manipulate magnetic interactions, opening doors for innovative applications in magnonics and spintronics.

A beneficial approach for gathering large datasets while maintaining user anonymity is federated learning. The main challenge with using this approach is keeping models consistent across different devices. This is particularly hard when dealing with changes in data distribution or when new classes need to be incorporated from various sources. We investigated the problem of adapting federated learning in mobile sensing applications with novel categories. The traditional federated learning technique lacks in handling appearing new categories due to its reliance on prior knowledge of class labels. Hence, it is not sufficient in covering diverse applications such as speech, environment, and activity recognition where new categories can't be anticipated in advance. This paper presents ZSFT, a zero-shot federated learning technique capable of handling appearing new categories without requiring any additional training. ZSFT uses a central aggregator to average both model weights and novel class labels. The novel class labels are gathered from users' devices but kept confidential from the aggregator. We tested ZSFT on various novel category scenarios and compared it against conventional federated and transfer learning approaches. The experimental results show that ZSFT outperforms other methods by significantly reducing testing accuracy loss due to the appearing novel categories.

The high-dimensional entanglement of multiple particles offers unique opportunities for conducting experiments that demonstrate nonlocal phenomena and related studies in quantum mechanics. In this article, we examine 4n+1-dimensional entanglement among n pairs of particles and present a comprehensive method for verifying the GHZ state via partial measurements. This method allows for identifying the complete set of unitary operations transforming the initial state into the target entangled state. We develop an efficient computational algorithm to determine this operational set for given measurement bases and propose a practical approach for implementing the target operations using available resources. The article illustrates the feasibility of this proposal with numerical results from experiments involving three pairs of particles and the associated technical requirements.

This research paper introduces a novel approach to wireless communication systems utilizing a reflective surface, aiming to mitigate channel estimation difficulties in complex scenarios like massive MIMO systems and mobile applications. A proposed solution involves a cascade channel estimation method that combines traditional channel estimation techniques. Simulation results demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency in terms of computational complexity. Furthermore, this concept can be applied to various scenarios, such as RIS-assisted multi-user systems, and its performance is evaluated and outperformed alternative solutions.

This study analyzes how regional news outlets covered the COVID-19 pandemic in the early stages and examines the associations between coverage, outbreak metrics, and audience response. Utilizing a diverse dataset of articles from four major US news agencies, including over 300 publishers in 220 markets, this research classifies news items into seven categories: COVID-Related, Economy-Related, Political, Other-Negative, Other-Positive, Neutral, and Undetermined. Our findings reveal variations in the scope of coverage across different types of publishers and regions. There is no correlation between the intensity of COVID-Related coverage and the severity of the pandemic in a particular area. Some regions with high COVID fatality rates received less COVID-Related coverage, suggesting a potential inverse relationship. The intensity of COVID-Related coverage is found to affect the amount of other news categories in a region, with areas having more COVID-Related coverage reporting less Economy-Related and Political news and more Undetermined content. Additionally, we discover that areas with more COVID-Related coverage experienced higher audience engagement, as measured by newspaper circulation and online traffic.

A recent study on mathematical counting indicates that individuals with mathematical expertise possess mental representations that evolve over time, accommodating new knowledge and displaying memory from previous exposures. In the cognitive sciences, a similar concept is referred to as a statistical theory of learning. We apply a machine learning approach to simulate the cognitive processes involved in counting. We utilize a memory-augmented recurrent neural network to model the sequential nature of counting, and evaluate the effectiveness of distinct memory update functions, back-to-front and front-to-back, in replicating the characteristic patterns observed in human counting data. We find that a hybrid approach that combines both methods outperforms individual methodologies in accurately predicting counting times. Moreover, we demonstrate that the proposed model is capable of accurately predicting both correct counts and incorrect counts made during the counting process. We validate the model's efficacy by comparing it to human counting data using various metrics, including mean absolute error and the multiple correlation coefficient.

Bloom filters provide fast membership tests for large sets of data, but they occasionally return false positives. Cuckoo filters offer an improved false positive rate, but at a higher memory cost. Xor Filters provide both faster membership tests and lower memory requirements compared to Bloom and Cuckoo filters. They utilize hash functions with specific properties to enhance performance. A membership test in Xor Filters involves calculating the parity of set elements' bits and comparing it to the parity of stored bits. This test takes only a few operations. A detailed explanation of Xor Filters' design and an efficient implementation are included. Performance benchmarks also demonstrate that Xor Filters strike an optimal balance between memory usage, false positive rates, and membership test speed.

Convex geometry and complex analysis have underlying connections with discrete mathematics. This short course will explore specific relationships between these fields. No advanced mathematical knowledge is required as the intensity will be beginner-friendly. The course will cover a range of topics, including alpha-convex bodies, holomorphic projections of function norms, and the geometric mean of operators within convex geometry and its applications in free convolution problems within probability theory.

A key inquiry in finance, spanning centuries, seeks to uncover past transaction trends that can foretell future market behavior, ultimately guiding investment decisions. Although numerous studies have focused on analyzing individual stock prices, this work delves into the analysis of transaction sequences to uncover hidden patterns indicative of impending market shifts. Our study introduces two novel, high-performance methods for detecting anomalous trends in time-series data, grounded in machine learning algorithms. Extensive simulation testing on artificially generated sequences reveals that these algorithms can pinpoint atypical patterns with exceptional accuracy. When applied to actual market data, these methods identify distinct patterns, confirming that market trends can be predicted based on prior transaction history.

This work presents FLVoogd, a robust federated learning framework capable of withstanding malicious participation and protecting user privacy. Specifically, FLVoogd incorporates several security features: 1) a framework for detecting and mitigating malicious users; 2) a method for automatically detecting and resolving model parameter corruption caused by malicious activity; 3) a strategy for gradually deactivating malicious users and adjusting the learning rate to prevent them from dominating the aggregation process; 4) a mechanism that effectively handles client dropout and prevents it from impacting model performance. Additionally, FLVoogd utilizes cryptographic techniques to shield user updates and aggregate them while maintaining partial visibility to prevent the formation of a global model that could compromise user privacy. Experimental results on a computer vision task demonstrate the effectiveness of FLVoogd in Federal learning applications.

Achieving autonomous driving in real-world scenarios is a complex challenge that can be tackled by bridging the gap between simulated environments and real-world conditions. This research focuses on the navigation module, specifically the loop-closure problem in mapping, and develops a solution by introducing gradient-based image features that resemble real-world image characteristics when replicated in simulated scenarios. Moreover, a new method is implemented to assign computed poses to sensor data, ensuring alignment with the simulated environment through gradient matching. This approach is evaluated in two key aspects: the reduction of sim-to-real distortion and the optimization of loop closure strategies. Experimental results using a SUIT car and a GT1080e camera demonstrate the efficacy of this method in real-world applications.

Deepfake technology has advanced significantly with state-of-the-art deep learning models, allowing for the creation of near-indistinguishable deepfakes. Our research focuses on the production and detection of strong deepfakes, which exhibit unique characteristics that set them apart from regular deepfakes. Unlike conventional deepfakes, these fake videos are created with real lip movements captured through 3D sensors but paired with incorrect audio. Our novel deepfake detection approach leverages a domain adaptation technique from computer vision to effectively analyze video spatial and temporal dynamics. Our method has yielded outstanding performance, particularly on YouTube deepfake challenge and Deepfake Detection 2.0 benchmark sets.

The identification of hidden oceans within sub-Neptune exoplanets holds key implications for understanding the formation and evolution of these planets. Current methods, however, often rely on infrarred emission signals that require highly precise measurements and are sensitive to thermal states but may not always reflect the actual mass of hidden oceans. An alternative approach is presented here, which proposes the use of distinct transit patterns caused by the dissolution of volatile species in a sub-Neptune's mantle, versus the separation of gases within the mantle and core. By analyzing the solubility-driven and gas-separation-driven transit signals, the mass of hidden oceans can be estimated, and the primary contributor to the planet's radius can be identified. Notably, the solubility signal is more sensitive to smaller masses of hidden oceans, and can provide complementary constraints that may help distinguish between different planetary formation scenarios.

A key goal for artificial neural networks inspired by the biology of the brain is to achieve learning mechanisms that align with natural processes, using the network's internal dynamics to store information over time, like our memory. This requires developing training methods that enable networks to learn in a realistic, brain-like manner. We propose a novel algorithm for spiking neural networks that makes use of a derivative-free gradient descent method, incorporating automatic weight updating and synapse modulation, without needing expensive backpropagation. This approach is unique as it doesn't need derivative computation and allows network parameters to be adjusted based on the strength of connections between different neurons. When tested using EEG data for predicting cognitive states, our method showed superior performance compared to standard training methods. Additionally, our results indicated that the network's internal parameters converged to realistic brain-like values, with our algorithm resulting in networks that function similarly to the human brain.

This paper outlines the results and methodologies employed in the 2021 ACL workshop challenge focused on handling out-of-vocabulary words within and outside of a language model's knowledge base. The challenge consisted of two parts: initially, we created a diverse word set consisting of 36k English words, which resulted in an average word set size of 1800 words per batch. Participants were presented with batches containing a sentence, a replacement token indicating a missing word, and a list of candidate words. The goal was to select the most appropriate word from the candidate list to maximize semantic coherence with the sentence. We utilized two datasets: Wikipedia sentences and OpenWebText sentences, for a total of 50 million training examples, as well as 38 million testing examples. The top-performing models integrated information from both the language model and candidate words, utilizing both supervised and unsupervised approaches to leverage the two sources effectively.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random outcomes and their associated spatial, temporal, and parameter dependencies.

However, the primary challenge lies in determining the necessary number of orthogonal basis functions to include in the expansion, as including too few would result in inadequate approximations, while including too many would lead to overly complex models with unnecessary details.

In the context of chaos expansions, legitimacy is confirmed by comparing the approximation to the original solution through direct computation, but this approach is impractical due to its exponential computational requirements.

This study presents a novel method for verifying the accuracy of chaos expansions by leveraging the properties of conservative differential equations, such as preserving certain physical attributes. The method involves testing for the preservation of these properties in the approximate solution, and if this is found to be deficient, adding additional basis functions to the expansion and re-evaluating until the desired level of accuracy is achieved.

This approach not only resolves the long-standing issue of determining the required number of basis functions, but it also offers a flexible framework for adaptively refining the approximation as needed. The method is demonstrated to work effectively in a range of case studies involving various types of differential equations.

In the field of data analysis, particularly statistical process control, researchers face a significant challenge due to the impact of variations in data quality. To address this issue, a new method called APOSAII has been developed to identify and isolate individual variations in large datasets. APOSAII leverages an adaptive metric that effectively captures correlation and scale information, making it capable of detecting changes in data even when they are univariate or have mixed dependency types. Furthermore, this metric's dynamic nature enables APOSAII to dynamically monitor and adjust for emerging differences as they occur. Through simulation studies and real-world applications, it has been demonstrated that APOSAII can accurately identify variations even in complex datasets with up to 100,000 data points. Notably, this approach performs comparably to other specialized methods even when those methods are specifically designed for specific data patterns or scenarios.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of six ultra-faint dwarf galaxies - known as the "fossil galaxies" that date back to the early universe - to gain insights into their early formation histories and chemical compositions. By using advanced star-formation models and simulations, we were able to identify and remove distorted light effects, allowing us to study the galaxies more accurately. The subsequent analysis revealed distinct patterns of metal enrichment across the galaxies, ranging from steady and uniform patterns to more complex patterns with differences in metal content. By comparing the observed patterns to simulations, we were able to rule out any distortion caused by the galaxies' orbits and instead point to the role of accretion - the process of galaxies merging - as the primary driver of these patterns. Furthermore, we were able to determine mass ranges for an unseen galaxy that may be responsible for this accretion, as well as constraints on the minimum mass required for such accretion events at early ages. By modeling the rates of accretion and star-formation, we were able to map the mass evolution of these galaxies over time, revealing a complex interplay between accretion and star-formation that may vary significantly from one galaxy group to another.

We define a spectrum of generalized cohomology theories for profinite groups by utilizing continuous finite-length $\mathbb{Z}_p$-modules and establish key properties. These properties include equivalence to the Borel spectrum in certain cases and an isomorphism for finite groups, as well as a reduction theorem for group extensions. Furthermore, we extend the Borel spectral sequence to a broad class of profinite groups and demonstrate that it possesses a fixed-point theorem.

Document analysis plays a vital role in a wide range of applications, but data labeling is often the most expensive expense in developing computer vision models, especially those that require detailed and precise annotations for complex document types. A new framework significantly reduces data labeling costs by switching from detailed labeling and incorporating simple, inexpensive text-based annotations instead, allowing fully automated and free labeling of large datasets. This approach leverages the power of pre-trained language models to effectively process text-based annotations, outperforming existing methods with only a minor loss in performance. As a result, this innovative method radicaly reduces data labeling expenses for visually rich document analysis frameworks.

The interface electronics of EuS/InAs heterostructures have been explored in depth using a range of surface analysis techniques. By varying the substrate orientation of InAs and introducing a buffer layer to break chemical bonds, samples have been produced with different interfaces between EuS and InAs. X-ray diffraction and magneto-optical spectroscopy show that the magnetic properties depend on the interface electronics, with differences observed across samples. Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry and atomic force microscopy have also been used to examine the samples' compositions and surfaces.

A reduction method in mathematical logic can compare computability properties of infinite sequences. Using this reduction, we can group such sequences into similar categories and study their computability. An important tool in this context is the Borel Wadge collapse, which provides a hierarchical organization of these sequences. We have developed an alternative classification system that is more detailed and is aligned with the collapsing order. This new system is efficient, as it allows us to determine the position of any sequence relative to any other sequence in linear time. Additionally, our classification system helps to identify key properties of sequences and their complements within this hierarchical framework.

Deep learning models have seen significant growth in their size due to the advancements in computing power and memory capacity. However, the process of training these models is becoming increasingly time-consuming, posing a significant challenge. To mitigate this issue, model pruning has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance inference efficiency and accelerate training time. There have been two primary types of pruning approaches: weight pruning and activation pruning. Weight pruning aims to eliminate redundant weights, while activation pruning focuses on eliminating unnecessary neurons. Both methods have inherent limitations - weight pruning can result in the loss of critical weights when combined, and activation pruning may lead to the loss of entire neurons. In this paper, we present ClickTrain, a novel pruning framework that combines architecture-preserving pruning of both weights and activations without losing any neuron or weight. ClickTrain employs a primary pruning layer to identify and delimit the neurons with active gradients, then allows only these neurons to transmit signals to secondary pruning layers that efficiently and precisely prune weights across all layers. By utilizing a lookup table to accurately track and prune weights without affecting model architecture, ClickTrain achieves precise pruning. Our experimental results show that ClickTrain yields high precision and efficiency, outperforming existing pruning methods by a significant margin.

We have expanded the model theory of the Distributive Complete Lambek Calculus with Modal Functions (dclm) to include Kripke semantics for modalities. This development allows us to leverage results from modal logic to characterize dclm modal logics as conservative or not conservative, depending on whether the underlying modalities are redundant. Additionally, we've identified two types of dclm modal logics: those with modalities that can be eliminated and those with irreducible modalities. Our work builds on the classification of non-associative modal logics by Aguilera, Bistue, and Galves.

The convergence of GW and EM signals from merging compact binaries holds the key to delivering fundamental insights into high-energy astrophysics and the severe conditions that lead to these events. By optimizing the detection of GW-EM mergers, researchers can gain valuable access to observational tools for the investigation of these phenomena. A novel method for accurately identifying and classifying GW signals produced by merging compact binaries has been introduced, allowing for precise determination of binary component types and masses. This method has been successfully simulated on real GW data from the first two observing runs of LIGO-Virgo, and has achieved remarkable performance in reproducing the recovery results of the Broey collaboration's GW-EM search. Furthermore, this approach can serve as a valuable resource for numerous such searches by providing valuable training data, and is capable of supporting various types of GW-EM searches by offering customizable classifiers for distinct analysis requirements.

A new member has been added to the small cluster of ancient giant exoplanets like HD 189733 and WASP-11. This new planet, named TOI-5542b, was discovered by the TESS telescope during a long-term survey. Based on a follow-up study using the APOGEE-2 spectroscopic survey, researchers determined the age of the TOI-5542 star system to be approximately 7 billion years. TOI-5542b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet that orbits its host star at a close distance, completing an orbit every 7.2 days. With an estimated mass similar to that of Jupiter, TOI-5542b is one of the least massive planets of its size discovered so far. Due to its high surface temperature, TOI-5542b is likely composed of a core surrounded by a thick envelope of gas that is slowly losing heat. This new discovery is unusual because the star it orbits around is metal-deficient and was formed 7 billion years ago, yet it still harbors a hot Jupiter planet. This poses a question as to the factors that contributed to the formation of TOI-5542b.

Restricted Markov Decision Processes (RMDPs) are a type of Markov Decision Process (MDP) with additional constraints limiting the state-action pairs that can be transitioned into. In particular, RMDPs are utilized in problems involving location-dependent constraints, such as traffic navigation with lane and intersection restrictions. A new approach based on linear programming is presented to find optimal policies for RMDPs, taking advantage of more efficient off-the-shelf software solutions. This method leverages the primal-dual least-quarestimation algorithm (PDLQ) and is comparable to other state-of-the-art RMDP solvers. The analysis demonstrates that PDLQ's solution quality declines linearly with the number of constraints. Moreover, PDLQ can benefit from simplifications, such as early termination, yielding significant improvements in runtime efficiency. The method is evaluated using real-world traffic navigation examples, with an emphasis on the effects of constraint complexity on runtime and solution quality.

This research addresses the challenge of Optical Character Recognition for math. Despite significant progress in machine learning, math OCR remains a complex task due to the diverse and ever-expanding set of math symbols. Our solution leverages the power of labeled data within the Labelbox platform to accurately recognize handwritten math equations from a sheet of paper. The unique framework combines a dataset of real-world, handwritten math samples sourced from the Math dataset on ImageNet with a custom designed math recognition model. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through rigorous testing on the Math dataset and a dataset comprised of actual handwritten math from chemistry students.

We examine bosonic quantum systems with their wavefunctions defined in lower-dimensional spaces, specifically one and two-dimensional spaces, and we study the extension of these systems to include supersymmetry. By mapping the systems to sheaf cohomology, we can compute higher cohomologies that arise from perturbations with fermionic charges. Our results indicate that these higher cohomologies can be expressed as products of fermionic condensates and topological invariants of the underlying bosonic system, and we provide concrete examples to illustrate our findings.

This study examines how interactions between components behave randomly and fluctuate in complex systems, and explores their implications for understanding stability. It presents a theoretical framework for analyzing and quantifying interaction variability. The theory is then applied to study the cell cycle, considering it as a complex network with interconnected components. This approach enables researchers to assess the cell cycle's stability by quantifying interaction variability and identify critical factors contributing to variability. This theoretical framework can be used to analyze and understand the behavior of other complex systems as well.

Actor-critic methods have become popular in reinforcement learning due to their efficient exploration of complex policy spaces. The critic, which uses a value function to guide the actor's policy search, significantly impacts its performance. One critical issue with actor-critic algorithms is the challenge in sampling actions that effectively exploit the current policy and estimate from the critic. This critical step is often poorly handled, leading to unoptimized action sampling. In this research, we present a novel approach that utilizes Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) to address action sampling. By leveraging HMC, the actor critic can efficiently sample actions that are based on an informed posterior, thereby facilitating more critical updates. The resulting algorithm is simple, readily applicable to existing actor-critic models, and outperforms the state-of-the-art in both theoretical and practical evaluations.

A fundamental demonstration of the Twin Prime conjecture can be given by utilizing the concept of a number's 'prime twinhood'. For any positive integer 'n', define f(n) as the smallest prime number greater than n that has a twin prime counterpart. Similarly, define g(n) as the largest prime number less than n that has a twin prime counterpart. It can be proven that if the Twin Prime conjecture is not true, then there exists a finite prime number 'q' such that f(n) and g(n) remain less than q for all 'n' greater than or equal to 2. This result stems from a fundamental demonstration of the Twin Prime conjecture.

Mobile robots navigating complex environments with limited visibility faces significant obstacles, primarily due to recurring collisions and delayed responses. Our research aims to enhance navigation efficiency and reliability for a robot moving through a layered environment on a map with varying terrain heights. To overcome visibility limitations, we have developed real-time sonar fusion software for a stratified mobile robot platform. The software uses ranging data from ultrasonic sensors to create a dynamic height-correlated map of the surroundings, which is then applied to navigate through confined spaces. The system has been thoroughly tested in real-time collision-navigated experiments within a 4x4 meter indoor environment.

We analyzed Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that has been observed to have a highly variable albedo pattern over the years. Our analysis of Nereid's reflectance properties observed in 1989 and 2020 reveals a notable decrease in the red spectral slope, suggesting a deep ice-rich layer on the surface of the satellite. However, this change may not necessarily indicate changes in the composition or distribution of water ice over time. Instead, it can be attributed to the presence of patches of pure ice overlapping with darker areas of the surface. When icy patches blend with other materials, they cause a notable decrease in the red spectral slope, but this effect can be reversed if they merge with patches of lower albedo. This phenomenon is responsible for the observed decrease in Nereid's red spectral slope between 1989 and 2020. Our analysis also reveals that the surface of the satellite exhibits spatial and temporal variations in the bound excess absorption feature at 1.5 micrometres, which is indicative of carbonates or chlorites. These variations may be the result of differing pathlengths of water ice or ice-rich patches over areas of darker material. Our findings have implications for future studies of Nereid, highlighting the need to use more targeted analysis methods that go beyond simple spectral decomposition of reflectance spectra.

Consider the set $\mathcal{M}_n$ of lower triangular matrices with entries from the ring $R_0$ and let $F$ be a quotient field of $R_0$. Denote by $\mathcal{P}_F^n$ and $\mathcal{P}_R^n$ the sets of matrices of size $n\times n$ with entries from the field $F$ and ring $R_0$ respectively. A projective line in the space of matrices $\mathcal{P}_F^n$ or $\mathcal{P}_R^n$ is defined as any subline that passes through the identity element. In our study, we examine surfaces in the space of affine transformations of the form $\begin{pm} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{pm}$ and projective line correspondences in the space of matrices of the form $\begin{pm} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{pm}$. These transformations and projective line correspondences arise from the action of the group $GL_n(R_0)$ on pairs $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B})$ consisting of invertible matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ with entries from the ring $R_0$. We propose a Tukey-type sequence framework, built upon insights from Pawlikowski's work, and use this structure to address questions regarding minimal cardinalities of models for first-order arithmetic. We also offer simplified proofs of certain theorems regarding the existence of independent families within certain cardinalities of subsets.

In the context of a dynamic treatment framework, policy evaluation becomes complex due to the challenges posed by missing data and positive self-selection. This study highlights the advantages of pessimistic optimization, a methodological framework that utilizes counterfactual models to mitigate these issues in policy simulation and optimization. However, pessimistic optimization is often seen as a conservative approach. This research introduces a novel Bayesian learning strategy for counterfactual models that is informed by actual treatment and outcome data, with the goal of enhancing pessimism's applicability to dynamic settings. The proposed strategy is initially evaluated in scenarios involving continuous and categorical treatments and outcomes, and then applied to real-world data from two studies examining the effects of health care interventions.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras are explored in detail. Specific instances of such dualities include Serre duality and Tanaka duality. The applications of these dualities to homological invariants are also examined, revealing how certain invariants become dual with respect to this phenomenon. Moreover, the duality theory is utilized to establish connections between homological invariants and algebraic-K-theory, as well as to interpret Nakayama algebras via this lens.

A graph state construction utilizing the complexification of the $E_8$ root system in eight-dimensional space has been developed, allowing the creation of quantumely entangled states based on a variety of configurations. By embedding $E_8$ within a larger Lie algebra, such as $F_4$, different subalgebras can be formed, leading to diverse graph state configurations. These constructions serve as a physical manifestation of the nontriviality of quantum contextuality, illustrating the complexity that arises when algebras are subjected to subfactor transformations.

In a study of one-dimensional interacting spinful fermion systems with topologically protected flat band using the density-matrix renormalization group method, it's observed that multi-body superconductivity arises in systems with specific interactions that favor three-body interactions. This finding contradicts a previous prediction that two-body interactions alone can lead to superconductivity in such systems. Notably, the optimal interaction strength that induces superconductivity below a certain temperature is much lower when three-body interactions are present. This suggests that multi-body interactions can significantly impact superconductivity in such systems, potentially making it more feasible to achieve superconductivity in such systems experimentally.

The classical Polya's theorem describes the distribution of prime factors among a sequence of natural numbers, starting from 2. We've extended this to a set of real numbers represented as rational functions in a field of size p, under a specific assumption about its polynomial ring.

This research investigates the performance of different clustering approaches applied to univariate, multivariate, and mixed data sets of existing or non-existent items, particularly in the context of state spatio-temporal patterns of species distribution. Various criteria are used to assess the quality of each cluster, including the consistency based on the number of observations, Calinski-Harabasz index, Calinski index, Davies-Bouldin ratio, C-index, Silhouette Width, and the number of clusters. Our analysis utilizes actual data sets from two studies on species distribution patterns. Three data sets from a study on the distribution patterns are used to compare the results of hierarchical clustering methods, including those utilizing the Ward, single link, and average link algorithms. Additionally, this study applies and compares the performance of Gaussian Mixture Modeling and Dirichlet Process Gaussian Mixture Modeling on the actual data sets.

In real-world scenarios, humans can easily identify salient items in complex environments, and this ability is crucial for various computer vision tasks, but current methods fall short due to incomplete or inaccurate learning targets, leading to subpar performance. To bridge this gap, we develop a novel task called salient item identification (SII), which involves pinpointing prominent items in both RGB and RGB-D images. To address the challenge of limited annotated data for SII, we propose a data-driven approach that utilizes domain-adaptive image generation to obtain more reliable synthetic labels. Additionally, we leverage class-aware feature learning to incorporate domain-agnostic knowledge and enhance model generalizability. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the outstanding performance of our proposed method on the SII task, and it is available at https://github.com/ChenChenPI/SSAIS.

The 2019 SemEval Offensive Language Task focused on identifying derogatory or offensive content within English tweets. Our system, UM-IU@LING, participated in the competition by developing models to address two subtasks: detecting derogatory language and identifying specific types of derogatory content. For subtask A, we utilized BERT and SVMs in a 10-fold cross-validation framework, while our subtask B model leveraged a pre-trained BERT-based model with 11 categories and was tested on a single annotation fold. Our final submissions incorporated both models to maximize our score.

For the natural number $4k+1$, where $k\geq 0$, in the set $\{0,1,\ldots,10^4-1\}$, we calculate the probability that the number's fourth power has a palindromic or antipalindromic representation in the standard base-$10$ system, or when expressed in the dyadic base-$10$ system with the digit-set $\{0,1,2,3\}$. We then determine the analogous probability for the number $2k$, when it falls within the specified range, and finally derive explicit formulas for the associated counting functions, which enable us to verify previously provided estimates by Bruckman, along with obtaining novel asymptotic expressions for the respective counting functions.

Computed Tomography (CT) plays a significant role in diagnosing and treating abdominal aortic aneurysms as well as other conditions affecting the vascular system and surrounding soft tissues. Since X-rays interact differently with various energy levels, and since medical imaging devices often employ polyenergetic X-ray sources, accurately reconstructing images requires taking into account how X-rays at different energy levels are absorbed by the subject being imaged. Formulating a complete forward model for this process is challenging due to its inherent computational complexity. As an alternative, iterative algorithms can be used to refine an initial image estimate towards a more accurate outcome by iteratively applying forward and inverse modeling steps. These algorithms typically result in a well-reconstructed image that closely matches the actual data being collected, but they can be computationally demanding and may struggle with noise present in the collected data. As an alternative to using a complete forward model, simplified models may be used that are less accurate but computationally more manageable. However, this may come at the cost of degraded image quality in the reconstructed image. A possible solution to these problems is proposed in the presented study. By combining total variation regularization with a simplified model and an additional constraint that accounts for energy levels, a non-convex optimization problem is formulated that yields a well-regularized and breakdown-resistant image. The effectiveness of this approach is confirmed by simulations and actual patient data.

Handwritten text recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of annotated data and limited language vocabulary. The success of recent advances in end-to-end HTR models heavily relies on the extensive use of synthetic data generated through automatic means. Nonetheless, existing approaches often fail to efficiently utilize available labor during training, resulting in subpar performance when evaluating real-world applications. To address this issue, this research presents a novel single-shot synthetic data generation technique that creates a substantial amount of data with minimal computational requirements, thus effectively incorporating manual annotations.
